As the meaning took shape, a cold feeling crept down his spine, and the room seemed to grow darker around him. The secret was solved, and he wished with all his heart that it were not.

The message, read from the last letter to the first, was written in a Latin that was short and almost casual. It told the bold traveller to descend into the crater of Snæfells Jökull, which the shadow of Scartaris touches before the end of June, and promised that he would reach the centre of the Earth. At the end stood a short line saying that the writer himself had done it, followed by his name.

Axel was struck cold with terror, because he knew his uncle well enough to guess what he would do with such a secret. In a moment of blind panic, he held the paper over the glowing fire, determined that the dreadful sentence should never be read by Lidenbrock. The edge of the page had already begun to curl and darken in the heat, and a thin smell of burning rose into the air.

At the very last second Axel snatched the paper back, for he could not bring himself to burn a treasure of such age and wonder. He folded it small, slipped it into the lining of his coat, and swore silently that his uncle should never hear a word of it. It was a noble resolution, but it was not destined to last through a single night of hunger and worry.

The night dragged by in the airless study, and the Professor paced up and down, muttering, tearing his hair and growing wilder with every hour of failure. Axel dozed uneasily in his chair, waking now and then in a cold sweat, and each time he felt a little weaker than before. Outside, in the silent streets of the great city, the lamps of Hamburg went out one by one.

By the following morning, Axel was so faint with hunger that the whole room seemed to swim before his eyes. He could not bear to see the old man's suffering any longer, and he could not bear his own, so in a thin voice he said that he had found the answer. It was the hardest sentence that he had ever spoken in all his short and anxious life.

The Professor snatched the paper from his hand, read the message aloud with growing amazement, and his face blazed with joy. He leapt about the study like a boy of ten, waving the page over his head, and for a moment Axel feared he would be crushed in an enormous hug. Never in all its long years had that tall old house seen such a happy man.

At last Lidenbrock unlocked the door and threw it open, and Martha hurried in with the dinner that had been waiting for a whole day. The Professor ate as though he had never seen food before, and between mouthfuls he laughed, quoted Latin and slapped the table with delight. Axel, meanwhile, ate in silence, with a heavy feeling in his heart and no real taste in his mouth.

Between two mighty helpings, the Professor explained that Saknussemm had gone down into the Earth through a volcano in Iceland, and had come back to tell the tale. He tapped the map with his fork, and declared with perfect calm that the two of them would follow the alchemist's footsteps. Axel, who had just been about to swallow a large mouthful of meat, very nearly choked on it.

Axel protested that the deeper one descends into the Earth, the hotter it becomes, until at some depth the very rocks must melt into liquid fire. He said that no man could survive in such a furnace, and he begged his uncle to remember the plain laws of science. It was a sensible and well-argued speech, and it made no impression on the Professor whatever.

Lidenbrock waved his hand and replied that nobody on Earth really knew what lay beneath the crust, and that the greatest scientists disagreed with one another about it. The only way to settle the matter, he said, was to go and see, and they would leave within a few days. Axel went to bed that night with the strong feeling that his life had been turned upside down.

That night Axel could not sleep, and when at last he did, he dreamed that he was falling through a bottomless dark pit. His uncle's voice called to him from far above, growing fainter with every second of the fall. He woke with a cry, drenched in sweat, and lay listening to his heart until the first grey light appeared at the window.

At the first opportunity he sought out Grauben in the garden and told her everything, from the old book to the strange message. He described the volcano, the plan and his uncle's fierce delight, and he waited for her to cry out in alarm. Instead she heard him to the end with a calm face and a thoughtful, steady gaze.

To his astonishment, Grauben showed no fear, and she told him quietly that a man of science must be ready to go wherever knowledge leads. She promised to wait for him in Hamburg for as long as it might take, even if the months turned into years. She urged him to come back with honour, and with a great story to tell his children.

Meanwhile, Lidenbrock collected instruments for the journey with the speed of a man who cannot bear to wait. He bought a chronometer to keep the time, a thermometer to measure the heat and a gauge to weigh the pressure of the air. Last of all came a fine compass, which was to show them the way through the dark.

They also packed coils of strong rope, iron-tipped climbing sticks, pickaxes, guns and a large supply of food for many weeks. The Professor insisted on carrying electric lamps rather than candles, since he was certain that the foul air of the depths would put an ordinary flame out. Axel privately wished that he could feel as certain of anything as his uncle felt about everything.

Lidenbrock visited a banker and came away with a letter of credit that would supply him with money in Copenhagen and in Iceland. Martha, who had been told almost nothing, filled the trunks with food and clean shirts and sniffed loudly over every one of them. By the evening the hall was so crowded that nobody could walk through it.

On the morning of their departure Martha stood at the front door with tears running down her cheeks, quite certain that two grown men had lost their minds. She said so to the postman, the milkman and anyone else who would listen. She went on saying it long after the carriage had rolled away down the street.

On their last evening together, Grauben gave Axel a small keepsake and promised that she would be waiting when he returned. Axel held her hand for a long time in the soft light of the garden. He found that none of the words he knew was big enough for such a goodbye.

Early the next day the two travellers boarded the train that would carry them out of Hamburg towards the north. Axel leaned from the carriage window and waved to Grauben until she shrank to a tiny spot and then vanished altogether. Only then did he sit down, with a heavy heart and a handkerchief pressed to his eyes.

At Kiel they went aboard a steamer called the Ellenora, which carried them across the water to Korsör on the coast of Denmark. The crossing was smooth and the sky was kind, so that the Professor stood happily at the rail the whole way. For the first time in many days, Axel felt something close to courage stirring in his chest.

The train carried them into Copenhagen, a handsome city of green towers, busy quays and wide, clean streets. Lidenbrock hardly looked at any of it, because his mind was already far ahead, on a mountain in Iceland. Axel, trotting behind him with the luggage, tried to remember what a calm holiday felt like.

The Professor went straight to the Museum of Northern Antiquities, where the curator, Professor Thomson, received him with open arms. Thomson loved old stones, old languages and old stories almost as much as Lidenbrock did. Within a few minutes the two scholars were talking like friends who had known each other for years.

Thomson told his visitors that a small ship, the Valkyrie, would soon be sailing for Reykjavik, the capital of Iceland. Obligingly, he wrote them letters of introduction to the governor of the island and to a teacher of natural science who lived in that town. Lidenbrock thanked him with a grin so wide that it seemed to split his face.

Lidenbrock was careful not to mention the parchment or his plan, even to so friendly and trustworthy a man. He said only that he wished to study the stones and volcanoes of Iceland, and the curator accepted the explanation with a polite nod. Axel, who was a very poor liar, studied the ceiling with great interest and held his tongue.

It suddenly occurred to Lidenbrock that Axel had always suffered from dizziness, and he resolved to cure it before they set out. He marched his nephew to the Church of Our Saviour, whose tall spire is circled on the outside by a spiralling staircase. Axel looked up at the thin stair, and his knees began to tremble before he had even set a foot on it.

Axel laid his hand on the rail and started to climb, but with every turn the staircase seemed to grow narrower and the wind stronger. The streets below shrank to the size of toys, and the whole city began to wheel slowly around him. He closed his eyes, pressed himself against the wall, and prayed for the climb to end.

At the very top, where a little golden ball stood above the roofs, the Professor forced Axel to stand upright and look down. For a long moment Axel kept his eyes shut tight, as if the world might disappear if he opened them. When at last he looked, he found that the city was still there, and that he had not fallen.

They climbed the spire again the next day, and the day after that, with the Professor shouting encouragement from behind. By the third morning, Axel could gaze down on the rooftops without turning pale, and he even enjoyed the wind in his face. Lidenbrock declared that it was a miracle of science, and took all the credit for it.

On the quay lay the Valkyrie, a small schooner with brown sails, which was being loaded with barrels, boxes and sacks. The captain greeted the travellers politely, although he seemed amused by the amount of luggage they had brought with them. He showed them a narrow cabin, hardly bigger than a cupboard, in which they were to sleep for the whole voyage.

As the Valkyrie slipped out of the harbour the wind was fair, and soon they sailed past a great old castle that guarded the narrow sea. Axel remembered that this was Elsinore, where the sad prince Hamlet had walked with the ghost of his father in the old play. The thought gave him a shiver, and he turned his eyes towards the open water.

As soon as the Valkyrie reached the open sea, Axel was overcome by a terrible seasickness. He lay in his narrow bunk for days on end, groaning, and he cared very little whether the ship sailed on or sank. The smell of tar and fish was more than his poor stomach could endure.

The Professor suffered from the same illness, but he was far too proud to confess it. He sat on the deck with a face the colour of old cheese, and he told everyone within hearing that a true scientist is never troubled by a few waves. A moment later, in the middle of this fine speech, he was sick over the rail like any ordinary passenger.

The wind rose, and the little schooner rolled and plunged through great grey waves while the sailors ran about with ropes and curses. Cold water splashed over the deck again and again, soaking the cargo, the sailors and the unhappy passengers alike. The captain, however, puffed calmly at his pipe and said that this was only a light breeze.

At last the wind dropped, and Axel's stomach calmed down enough to allow him to eat a little bread. He climbed up to the deck, wrapped in a blanket, and watched the sea birds that followed the ship in white, wheeling clouds. After so many days of misery, even the grey water seemed beautiful to him.

After about ten days of sailing, a low dark line appeared at the edge of the sea and slowly thickened. As the ship drew nearer, it became a rough and rocky coast, with white mountains rising behind it and mist curling about their feet. Axel realised, with a strange mixture of wonder and dread in his heart, that this was really Iceland at last.

The Valkyrie slipped into a small harbour and tied up beside a stone quay, with a great creaking of ropes. Reykjavik proved to be a poor little town of wooden houses, with grass and wild flowers growing on their roofs. Axel thought that it looked like a village out of a fairy tale, and in the pale northern light he was not far wrong.

Count Trampe, the governor, received his visitors in a plain office, wearing a simple coat and a pleasant smile. He read the letter from Professor Thomson with care, and then he promised that the people of Iceland would give the scholars all the help they could. Lidenbrock bowed so low in thanks that his nose very nearly touched the governor's polished wooden floor.

Next they called on Mr Fridriksson, who taught natural science at the school of Reykjavik, and who greeted them with great kindness. He spoke excellent Latin, and the Professor almost danced with joy, because he could not say a word of Danish. Axel, too, was glad, for it meant that he could finally understand a whole conversation again after so many silent days.

Lidenbrock asked at once whether the town library held any work by Arne Saknussemm, and the teacher shook his head sadly. Every writing of that learned man, he explained, had been burned in 1573 by order of the Church, which considered it a danger to the faith. The Professor stood there speechless and pale, as if he had been struck by a bolt of lightning from a clear sky.

Seeing the Professor's face fall, Mr Fridriksson led him to a large map of Iceland that hung on the wall. He pointed to Snæfells, a huge mountain in the west of the island, whose top is covered with a cap of ice. It was, he said, an old volcano, and nobody in the town could remember a time when it had last erupted or shaken the ground.

Mr Fridriksson told them that the best guide for the mountain was a man named Hans Bjelke, who earned his living by hunting eider ducks for their soft down. Lidenbrock was delighted at once, and he demanded to meet this Hans without wasting a single minute. He drummed impatiently on the table with his fingers, glared at the clock, and did not stop until the man was sent for.

The next morning a tall man with a fair beard and calm blue eyes appeared at the door of their lodging. He was broad in the shoulder and strong in the arm, and he studied the travellers as though he understood a great deal more than he ever said. Axel felt, without knowing why, that this man could be trusted with a life.

The Professor offered Hans three rix-dollars a week to guide them to the mountain, and then to wherever else they might wish to go. Hans said only one word, which was Ja, and that was the whole of the agreement. Lidenbrock, who usually argued over every coin, was so pleased that he shook the man's hand three times.

Axel tried to start a conversation with Hans in his poor Danish, asking about the road, the weather and the habits of the horses. Hans answered every question with a slow nod or a short grunt, and he never once showed any sign of being annoyed. Before an hour had passed, Axel had decided that he was the quietest man in the world.

They spent the day buying food and equipment in the little town, and the pile of boxes grew higher and higher. Hans inspected everything without a word, weighing each bundle in his hand with a look of mild disapproval. When the Professor forgot something important, Hans fetched it before he could even ask.

Hans also found the horses, and he tied the loads on to their backs so neatly that nothing could shift or fall. Axel watched him with growing admiration, for each knot was tied in the same patient, careful way. He began to feel that this silent man could solve any problem that the road might offer.

Mr Fridriksson came to see them off, and he wished them all the luck in the world, though he looked a little puzzled. He still could not understand why two foreign scholars were so eager to scale a mountain of ice. He was far too courteous to ask, and Lidenbrock was far too cautious to explain.

Early the next day they rode out of Reykjavik on small, shaggy Icelandic horses, which were sturdy, patient and astonishingly short. Axel's long legs almost trailed on the ground, and he felt rather like a man riding a large dog. The Professor laughed so hard at the sight that he nearly slid from his own saddle.

The road followed the coast across a bare black country of stones, moss and old lava, without a single tree to break the view. There were no houses and no travellers, and for hours the only sound was the soft tread of the horses on the stones. Axel had never seen a land so completely empty, or one so strangely and silently beautiful in its emptiness.

At nightfall they stopped at a farm, a low house of turf and stones with grass growing on its roof. The farmers shared their milk and dried fish with the strangers as though they were old friends, and they refused to take any payment. Axel went to sleep thinking that poor people are sometimes the most generous in the world.

After some hours of riding, they came to an arm of the sea that cut deep into the land and could not be avoided. There was no bridge and no road around it, so the three travellers stood on the shore and waited patiently. At last a small boat appeared on the grey water, rowed by two sunburned men.

Hans guided the horses into the boat with a quiet, steady hand, and the little craft pushed off and moved slowly across the water. Axel gripped the side with both hands and tried not to think about what would happen if the animals took it into their heads to move. The Professor, meanwhile, was busy studying the colour of the rocks on the far shore.

Whenever the road crossed a stretch of fresh black lava, Lidenbrock leapt down from his horse to pick up a stone. He turned each piece over in his fingers, named it aloud with great affection, and slipped it into his already overflowing pocket. Axel reckoned that by the end of the journey they would be carrying half of Iceland.

They rode on for several days, and Hans always knew precisely which way to go, though there was no path and no sign to be seen. He never consulted a map, he never asked a passing farmer, and he never once seemed troubled by doubt. It was as though the whole country were a book that he had read many times.

At last they came to Stapi, a tiny village by the sea that lay in the shadow of a huge and silent mountain. The pastor of the parish came out of his house at once, and he welcomed the weary strangers as warmly as if they had been old friends. Axel felt for the first time that Iceland might be a kind country after all.

The pastor was a poor man, but he was cheerful and generous, and he shared his supper and his only spare room without hesitation. The fish was dry and tough and the bed was hard as a board, yet Axel slept better than he had slept for weeks. All night, in his dreams, the great white mountain stood waiting outside the window like a patient and silent guest.

In the morning, Axel looked out of the window and saw Snæfells for the first time, rising above the roofs of the village. The mountain wore a cap of ice that shone against the pale northern sky like a crown of silver. It was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen, and the most frightening.

The pastor promised to look after the horses until their return, and the three men set out on foot with heavy bags on their backs. Hans carried the biggest share of the load himself, striding along as if it weighed no more than a feather. The Professor walked in front, humming happily to himself a tune that he had loved in his student days.

All day they climbed over black ash and loose stones, with patches of old snow and sheets of blue ice lying here and there among them. The air grew colder with every step, and the wind pulled at their coats, while Axel's breath came in short and tired puffs. Hans, however, climbed on steadily and carefully, and he said not a single word of complaint from morning to evening.

Late in the day they reached the summit, and there they discovered that the mountain had not one crater but three. Each was a deep, dark hole in the ground, like the mouth of some enormous sleeping beast, and a bitter wind howled across its edge. Axel looked down into the nearest, and he felt his knees begin to shake.

On the summit, Lidenbrock took out the message once more and read it aloud in the bitter wind, as if reciting a prayer. Then he walked slowly around the rims of the three craters, peering into each one in turn. His lips moved all the while, and Axel guessed that he was repeating the Latin words under his breath.

He explained to his nephew that the message named a high rock on the edge of the mountain, called Scartaris, which stood like a tower against the sky. Just before the end of June, its shadow would fall upon one of the three craters, and that crater alone was the doorway. Without the sun, however, there would be no shadow at all, and without a shadow there would be no door to open.

Since the shadow could appear only if the sun was shining, they had no choice but to wait for fair weather. They made a camp in a sheltered hollow close to the summit, and Hans quickly built a snug little hut out of loose stones and canvas. By evening it had stopped the worst of the wind, and even the Professor admitted that it was comfortable.

But the weather stayed foul, and for day after day nothing could be seen but swirling fog and cold, driving rain. The Professor grew gloomier with every passing hour, and he stopped speaking even of his beloved stones. His silence, Axel thought, was far worse than any of his loud and stormy speeches.

Axel lay awake in the damp hut, hoping with all his heart that the sun would never come and that they would be forced to go home. A moment later he felt ashamed of such a selfish and cowardly wish, and he turned his face to the wet canvas. Both of these thoughts followed him into his restless sleep, and they quarrelled there with each other all night long.

Each day Hans went out to hunt in the mist, and each evening he returned with birds, which he cooked over a small and smoky fire. He never complained of the delay, nor of the cold, nor of the strange behaviour of the men who had hired him. Axel envied the quiet, unshakable patience of the hunter, and wished that some of it might rub off on his own restless mind.

The Professor paced along the edge of the craters with his hands clasped behind his back, and every so often he shouted at the clouds. He seemed to believe that if he were only angry enough, they would take fright and drift away. The clouds paid him no attention at all, and they went on pouring cold rain steadily down upon his hat and his shoulders.

The days of June fell away one by one, and Lidenbrock counted them in his notebook with a worried and deeply lined face. If the sun did not appear very soon, he told Axel in a flat voice, then the message would be useless for another whole year. He could not bear to think of the long and weary waiting that would follow, with the whole winter ahead of them first.

At last, one morning, the fog thinned, the clouds opened like a curtain, and a golden sun climbed above the mountain. A long, sharp shadow fell from the tall rock called Scartaris, and it began to creep slowly across the three craters. Axel held his breath, and even the calm Hans stopped chewing his bread to watch.

The shadow reached the middle crater, stopped, and rested there like a long finger pointing at the heart of the mountain. Lidenbrock threw out his arms and shouted, in a voice that must have carried all the way to Stapi, that they were going forward to the centre of the Earth. Hans nodded, said his usual Ja, and without any further ceremony began to check the ropes and the packs one by one.

Early the next morning they fixed their ropes to a strong block of rock at the edge of the middle crater. Lidenbrock checked each knot twice and then once more, for he knew that a single slip could end the whole adventure in a moment. Axel pretended, as bravely as he could manage, that his own trembling was only a result of the early morning cold.

Hans lowered the heavy bags on a long rope, and then the three men began to climb down one by one into the darkness. The shaft was black and endless, and Axel could not see the bottom, which was perhaps just as well for his courage. Around him the walls were rough and cold, and every time he moved, the long rope creaked and groaned above his head.

The shaft was narrow and steep, and its walls of rough black lava scraped against their hands and knees with every move. Looking up, Axel watched the circle of sky grow smaller and smaller, until it shone like a bright coin at the end of a very long tube. Then he looked down into the darkness, which was worse, and he tried to keep his eyes fixed on his own hands.

After many hours of careful climbing, they reached the floor of the crater, and they found a gently sloping tunnel that led into the heart of the mountain. Lidenbrock raised his lamp, and the light ran far ahead along the passage and was swallowed by the dark. The way was open at last, he said, with a satisfied grin, and now nothing in the world could stop them.

They slept on the hard stone floor, huddled close together, with one of the electric lamps left burning beside them. Axel lay awake for a long time, because the silence inside the rock was so deep and complete that it hurt his ears. He listened to his own heartbeat in the dark, and he thought, in spite of himself, of the whole enormous weight of the mountain above him.

The next day they walked steadily downhill through a tunnel of ancient lava, which was as smooth and black as glass. Their lamps threw a bright circle of light around them, and beyond it the darkness waited like a living thing. Their footsteps echoed far ahead and far behind, so that it seemed that an invisible army was marching with them.

After a while the black lava gave way to bands of older rock in many different colours, laid one upon another like the pages of a huge book. The Professor named each kind with enormous joy, running his fingers over the stone as if he were greeting old friends in a foreign land. For him, as he cheerfully explained to Axel, every step downward was also a step backward in the long history of the world.

Lidenbrock studied the thermometer and then burst into loud laughter, because the heat had scarcely risen at all since they had entered the mountain. He declared that the learned men who had feared a burning furnace inside the Earth had been mistaken from beginning to end. Axel, who had made the very same argument himself only a few days earlier, could find nothing at all to say in reply.

Hans quietly checked the water in the flasks, and then he held up the small remaining supply with a worried look on his usually calm face. The Professor brushed the matter aside with a wave of his hand and said that a spring was certain to turn up on the way. Axel wished with all his heart that he could believe it as easily as his uncle did, and he said nothing.

A little further on, the tunnel divided into two branches, and each of them seemed equally dark, narrow and silent. After a moment's thought, Lidenbrock decided to follow the eastern branch, and he said it with the confidence of a man who had never made a mistake. Hans nodded, said nothing at all, picked up the heaviest of the bags and followed the Professor into the gloom.

In the eastern tunnel they came upon a thick seam of black coal, and Lidenbrock raised his lamp to the wall with a shout of delight. The stone was marked with the delicate prints of ferns, the leaves of vast forests that had grown and died long before there were any people on Earth. Axel touched them gently, as one touches the pages of a very old letter.

The days passed in a steady routine of walking, eating, sleeping and walking again, until the hours had lost all meaning in the endless dark. Lidenbrock wrote the depth in his notebook with great care every time the chronometer struck the hour. He looked more cheerful with every number that he wrote, while Axel grew more anxious.

The flasks of water grew lighter day by day, and Hans reported the problem in his own silent fashion by holding one up and shaking it. Lidenbrock ordered that each man should take only a few small mouthfuls a day, and for once nobody argued with him. The tunnel was dry, and the fear of thirst grew in them like a second shadow.

One morning the tunnel simply came to an end, for they had reached a wall of smooth, solid rock without a crack in it. There was no door, no hidden opening and no way through, and the Professor tapped the stone with his pickaxe in stubborn disbelief. The echo that came back was dull and flat, like the sound of a closed coffin.

Axel sank to the ground in despair, for he was certain that the mountain had tricked them and that they would never see the sun again. Lidenbrock was silent for a very long time, and his face seemed to age as Axel watched. At last he said only that they must go back and try the other way.

They marched back up the long tunnel, thirsty and tired, until they came at last to the place where the road had divided. There they took the western branch, which Lidenbrock had refused to follow before, and he did not say one word about his mistake. Axel, who had no strength left to be angry with him, was grateful for that silence.

After a long day of walking, Axel's tongue felt like a strip of dry leather, and at last his legs would carry him no further. He fell to his knees on the stones, and the Professor, with trembling hands, gave him the very last of the water from his own flask. It was the kindest thing his uncle had ever done, and neither of them spoke of it afterwards.

Hans stopped suddenly and laid his ear against the rock wall, as though he were listening to the heartbeat of a friend. After a moment he turned and said a single word, which Axel understood at once because it was the most beautiful word in the world, and it meant water. For the first time since they had met, his calm blue eyes were shining like a boy's.

The Professor pressed his own ear to the stone and heard a soft rushing sound, like a distant river running behind a door. They attacked the wall at once with pickaxes, and after a few minutes of hard work the rock gave way, and a bright stream of water burst out of it. It splashed over their boots, sparkling in the lamplight, and then it ran away down the tunnel into the dark.

The three men threw themselves down beside the stream and drank until they could drink no more, laughing and coughing like children. Lidenbrock named the stream the Hansbach in honour of their guide, and he announced the name with great pride, as if he had discovered a new continent. Hans looked at the water and then at the Professor, and seemed to think the whole matter rather foolish indeed.

For days they followed the Hansbach down a tunnel that grew steeper with every mile, until the walls themselves seemed to tilt forward. The stream was now their guide and their friend, and the sound of it never left their ears. Even the Professor admitted, with a grunt, that without it they would have been utterly and hopelessly lost in the mountain.

One evening Axel felt too tired to keep pace with the others, and he sat down on a rock to rest for a moment. The lamps of his uncle and the hunter moved on around a bend in the tunnel, growing smaller and smaller. Then they vanished, and Axel was left alone with the sound of dripping water.

He rose at once and hurried after them, following what he believed to be the path, but at a fork he took the wrong turn. Gradually the whisper of the stream grew fainter behind him, until at last he could hear nothing at all. Only then did it occur to him that he had no idea where he was.

Axel shouted for his uncle, and then for Hans, and then for anyone who might hear him, but nobody answered his cries. The only reply was the hollow echo of his own frightened voice, repeating itself again and again from the dark. He understood, with a sickening drop of the heart, that he was entirely alone.

He tried to hurry back the way he had come, but he stumbled over a loose stone, and his lamp flew from his hand and fell. It broke on the floor with a small sad crack, and at once the whole world turned black. He had never imagined that any man with open eyes could be made so completely and so terribly blind by the absence of light.

He sat down in the dark, and he had never known that darkness could be so total, so heavy, and so patient. He thought of Grauben waiting in the sunny garden at Hamburg, of the great blue sky, and of the immense weight of the mountain pressing above his head. It seemed to him that every one of these things was lost for ever.

He called his uncle's name until his throat was sore, but the rock gave back nothing but echoes, which died away into silence. Tears ran down his face, and he felt like a small child who had been forgotten in a great dark house. Nobody in the whole wide world knew where he was, and, as far as he could tell, nobody at all was able to help him.

Then, as he leaned wearily against the wall, he caught a sound so faint that he thought he had imagined it, like a voice speaking inside the stone. He pressed his ear to the rock, and slowly he understood that the wall of the gallery was carrying sound over a great distance. It was like a long whispering tube, and he was at one end of it.

Little by little he made out words, and with a leap of the heart he knew that it was his uncle's voice. Lidenbrock was telling him to keep calm and to keep brave, and to follow the slope downward until they could find each other. Each word took a long time to arrive, as if it were being carried across a wide and stormy sea.

Axel crawled to the edge of the slope and meant to go down slowly and carefully, but his feet slipped on the smooth stone. He slid faster and faster down the dark incline, with nothing to catch hold of, and the speed took his breath away. Then his head struck the rock with a dreadful crack, and a great black silence closed over him like deep water.

When Axel opened his eyes, he found himself cradled in the strong arms of Hans, who was carrying him calmly down the tunnel as if he weighed no more than a child. His uncle walked beside them with a lamp, and in its light he looked older and paler than Axel had ever seen him. For a long moment Axel thought that he must still be dreaming, and that the dream was a kind one.

Lidenbrock was so overjoyed to find his nephew alive that tears ran openly down his weathered cheeks, and he did not trouble to hide them. Axel begged his pardon for the trouble he had caused, and the old man waved the apology away with a trembling hand. Then the three of them lay down together in the tunnel and rested quietly for a full day without eating much.

After the rest they went on along the tunnel, which grew wider and brighter with every step, and the air grew fresher too. Then, quite suddenly, the walls fell away on both sides, and they stepped out into an enormous open space filled with a pale and steady light. For a long while nobody said a single word, because there was nothing in any language that could match what they saw.

Before them lay a vast sea as flat and silent as a mirror, and its far shore was too distant for any eye to see. High above, the roof of the cavern glowed like a cloudy grey sky, so that the whole scene looked like a morning on the coast of some unknown country. Axel had to remind himself, again and again, that they were many miles beneath the ground and far from every road.

Lidenbrock stood on the fine sand with his arms spread wide, like a conqueror on a newly won shore, and he named the water the Lidenbrock Sea. Axel, whose thoughts were far away at home, called the little bay where they stood Port Gräuben, and the Professor smiled and did not object. It seemed to the Professor a very good name for a harbour, and so the name was written into his notebook.

There was no sun in this strange world, and yet the whole cavern was bathed in light, which seemed to come from the air itself. Axel guessed that it was some kind of electricity glowing among the clouds, although he did not understand how such a thing could happen under the Earth. He wished, not for the first time in his life, that he had studied harder at school and listened to his teachers.

The air here was warm and thick and as easy to breathe as the air of a summer evening, which surprised everyone, and Axel most of all. They walked along the beach for hours, picking up pretty shells and looking out over the motionless water. It was very hard to remember, in such a peaceful place, that they were prisoners of the dark and had no way back.

Soon they came to a forest unlike any that grew on the surface of the Earth, for all of its trees were enormous pale mushrooms. Each one was as tall as a house, and their wide, flat caps made a soft roof over the heads of the three small men. The light that fell between their stems was greenish and strange, and it made the whole forest look like a dream.

Beyond the mushrooms they found a broad plain that was covered with bones, and many of them were as thick as the trunks of trees. Lidenbrock moved among them with shining eyes, naming one skeleton after another, and he declared that these were creatures that had died out thousands of years before. Axel followed behind him, trying very carefully not to step on the ancient past with his heavy boots.

Lidenbrock suddenly bent down and lifted a skull from the ground, and it looked remarkably like the head of a man. He announced that it proved that human beings had lived at the same time as the great animals, but Axel was far from sure. They argued about it all the way back to the beach, and neither of them won, for no one could say who was right.

As he walked beside the pale mushrooms, Axel suddenly saw something huge moving among the stems, far off in the green dimness. It looked like a giant of a man guarding a great herd of beasts with long, curving tusks, and Axel's blood ran cold. He turned and ran back to the others as fast as his legs could carry him.

Lidenbrock laughed and told his nephew that he was seeing things, which was easy to do in so strange a place, and he refused to go and look. They went back to the shore together, but Axel could not stop glancing over his shoulder at the dark trees. In the end he decided, a little sadly and rather wisely, that it would be better not to talk about it any more.

The shore offered no tunnel leading onward, nor any other way out, only high walls of rock and the endless sea. The Professor gazed at the water for a long time with his hands on his hips, and at last he declared that the road to the centre must lie across it. Axel could see by the set of his uncle's jaw that the matter was already settled, and that no argument would change it.

While the others were arguing, Hans wandered along the beach and came upon a great heap of black wood, washed up long ago. It was as hard as iron to the touch, and Lidenbrock explained that it came from ancient trees which had been slowly turned almost into stone. For the first time on the whole journey, the Professor thanked the hunter aloud and shook him warmly by the hand.

Hans set about building a raft, binding the heavy logs together with ropes and fitting them close so that no water could come between. Axel helped whenever he was told to, and for days the beach rang with hammering and the creak of rope. Lidenbrock, who could not build anything, walked up and down giving advice that nobody asked for.

At last the raft was finished, and it floated well in the shallow water, riding high and steady. Hans gave it a short mast, a sail cut from their blankets and a long oar that would serve as a rudder. It was a clumsy craft to look at, but it was strong and well made, and Axel could not help admiring it.

They loaded the raft with food, water, tools and guns, and each man had his own place to sit among the baggage. Lidenbrock wrote the date in his notebook with great ceremony, although nobody could be quite certain how many days had really passed. In that strange place of constant light, where there was neither sunrise nor sunset, time had lost its edges altogether.

Hans pushed the raft out of Port Gräuben with his oar, and the little sail filled with a gentle wind. Axel looked back and watched the shore dwindle behind them, with the strange feeling that he was leaving his last link with the world he knew. The mushroom forest grew smaller and smaller on the pale shore, and after a while it was gone from sight.

The days on the sea were calm, and the raft moved quietly forward, with Lidenbrock steering by the compass and his eyes on the far, dim horizon. He wrote in his log every few hours, although nothing happened except the slow movement of the clouds overhead. Axel, who had had quite enough of adventures for the moment, was perfectly content to let it stay that way.

One day Hans lowered a line with an iron hook into the water, and before long he pulled up a strange and heavy fish. It had a thick plate of bone over its head and its body, like a small knight in armour, and Lidenbrock declared with excitement that its kind had died out long ago. Hans, who was less interested in science than in supper, simply took out his knife and began to clean it.

That evening they cooked the strange fish on a small spirit lamp, and it tasted a great deal better than anyone had expected. Axel laughed, for the first time in days, and said that it was probably the oldest meal that any human being had ever eaten. Even Hans, who rarely showed any feeling at all, allowed himself the ghost of a smile as he ate.

Lidenbrock let down a heavy weighted line to measure how deep the sea was, and he paid out more and more rope with an intent and thoughtful face. When at last the line went slack, the markings showed that there was a vast depth of water beneath the raft. Axel decided, with a small shiver, that he would much rather not look down into all that darkness.

Some time later, while Axel was keeping watch, he saw a ripple spreading across the calm water far ahead of the raft. It was a slow and strange movement, as if something enormous were rising unhurriedly from the deep. A cold hand seemed to close slowly around his heart as he sat and watched the ripple draw nearer to the raft.

Then a huge head broke the surface, with eyes as big as dinner plates and a mouth crammed with long, sharp teeth. It was the head of a monster of a kind that had ruled the oceans of the world many millions of years earlier. Axel opened his mouth to scream for help, but only a thin and breathless squeak came out of it.

A moment afterwards a second creature rose from the water, with a long neck that swayed above the waves like the body of a giant snake. Axel found his voice at last and cried out to his uncle in terror, and the Professor and Hans looked up from their work. Hans, who had not been surprised by anything so far, went as pale as the foam on the waves.

The two monsters caught sight of each other, and in an instant they hurled themselves into a terrible battle of teeth and coils. The sea boiled and foamed around the little raft, and great waves lifted it high and dropped it again like a leaf. Axel clung to the mast with both arms, shut his eyes tight, and waited for the raft to be smashed to pieces.

Lidenbrock was so thrilled by the sight that he forgot to be afraid, and he pulled out his notebook and began to sketch with a trembling hand. Between the flying drops of spray, he noted each movement of the fight and named each beast aloud with childish delight. Axel, who was holding on for his life, thought that his uncle must have lost his senses entirely.

After a long and fearful struggle, both creatures suddenly dived and vanished beneath the surface, leaving only a patch of churning foam behind them. The water closed over them, and a whirlpool formed in the place where they had been, which spun the raft round and round like a toy. Hans fought against it with his long oar, and at last he steered them out of the circle of dangerous water.

At last the sea grew quiet again, and the three men sat very still in the middle of the great empty water. For a long time none of them spoke, because no words seemed large enough for what they had seen. Axel kept his eyes fixed on the place where the monsters had gone down, in case they should decide to come back.

Axel talked quietly with his uncle about the monsters, and Lidenbrock suggested that this was a hidden sea, where such creatures might have lived undisturbed for ages. Some hours later, they saw a tall column of water rising from the sea far ahead of them, like the jet of a mighty fountain. They steered the raft towards it at once, for Lidenbrock was eager to learn what kind of place could send up such a tower of water.

After some hours, the raft drew near to a small, rocky island, where a tall fountain of steaming water shot up from the stones with a roar. Lidenbrock leapt ashore at once, planted his boot on the wet rock, and announced that the island would be known as Axel Island. His nephew, who had never expected such an honour, blushed to the roots of his hair and said nothing.

The water of the fountain was so hot that none of them could bear to touch it, and its steam hung in a pale cloud above the sea. Lidenbrock measured the heat with his thermometer and wrote the number in his notebook with the greatest possible care. It was, he said, a fact that would delight every geologist in Europe, if only they could ever read it.

Axel felt a little proud, though he knew that nobody else would ever see this lonely island or read its name on any map. They pushed off from the rocks and sailed away, and the fountain slowly sank behind them, until it was only a white thread against the distant roof of the cave. The wide sea was empty once more, and the only sound was the soft whisper of the water against the logs.

Some days later, the roof of the cavern grew darker, and heavy clouds began to gather above the water. The light turned a dull, sullen grey, and the sea looked flat and cold, like a sheet of dark metal. Axel had a bad feeling that the calm of the past days had only been a pause before something worse.

Hans studied the sky for a moment with narrowed eyes, and then he lowered the sail and wrapped it tightly round the mast. He lashed down every box and every gun with quick, sure hands, and said not a word. Axel understood from his silence that something truly dangerous was coming towards them across the water.

The air grew thick and strangely still, and Axel felt the hair rise on his head as if an invisible hand were stroking it. From far away came a low, deep rumble of thunder that seemed to shake the whole cavern from its roof to its floor. Nobody on the raft moved or spoke, for every man there could feel that a great storm was gathering in the sky above.

Then the storm broke, and the wind howled across the sea with a voice like a thousand wolves, while the rain fell in sheets. The three men tied themselves to the mast with ropes, and the raft rose and fell among waves as tall as houses. Axel thought, as each new wave rose above him, that it must surely be the last one that he would ever see.

Balls of white fire danced across the planks of the raft, rolling about like living things, and the thunder was so loud that Axel could hear nothing else. The lightning split the sky again and again, and the whole sea shone with a hard blue light that hurt the eyes. It seemed to him that nothing on earth could be so loud, so bright and so frightening, and that it must be the end of the world.

Lidenbrock clutched the compass in his shaking hands, and he saw that the needle spun round and round like a mad thing. He wrote in his notebook that the lightning had made it behave in this way, but he did not for a moment guess what it might mean for their journey. That discovery, which would change everything, was still waiting for them somewhere further along the road.

At last a giant wave rose in front of them, higher than any that had come before it, and it seemed to hang over the raft like a black cliff. It lifted them up and up into a roaring darkness, and then the whole world turned to noise and blackness, and Axel knew nothing more. Even Hans, the calmest of men, had closed his eyes and was holding the mast with all of his great strength.

When Axel opened his eyes, the roaring had passed, and the raft lay stranded on a rocky shore that was washed by quiet waves. Hans was standing beside him with a hand on his shoulder, and he looked wet and weary but quite unhurt. It was a long time before Axel could believe that he was still alive.

The three men checked their baggage, and they found, to their great relief, that most of it had survived the storm. The food, the tools and the guns were safe, although a few small things had been swept away by the waves into the sea. Lidenbrock was far more concerned about his precious notebook, which was damp and crumpled but still, to his joy, quite intact.

While walking along the shore in search of firewood, Axel noticed something dark between two stones, and he bent down to look at it more closely. It was an old, rusty dagger, and it lay there as though somebody had dropped it long ago and never returned. He picked it up carefully with a feeling of awe, as one might lift something that belonged to a ghost.

Lidenbrock held the weapon up to the lamp and declared that it had been forged in the sixteenth century, which was the age of Saknussemm. He wondered aloud whether it might have belonged to the alchemist himself, and his eyes shone with a hope that Axel found alarming. Axel looked at the thick red rust that covered the blade, and he was not nearly so sure of anything.

They followed the shore beneath tall black cliffs, looking everywhere for some opening that would lead them onward and downward. The rocks were wet and slippery, and every few minutes the Professor stopped to study them through his glasses with a look of deep suspicion. Hans followed behind them with the heaviest of the heavy bags on his back, and he said nothing at all about it.

Presently they came to the mouth of a tunnel, and there Axel noticed two letters cut deeply into the rock beside it. They were an A and an S, the initials of Arne Saknussemm, and the strokes looked old, worn and carefully made. Nobody had been here since the alchemist himself, it seemed, and the rest of the whole world had forgotten the place.

The Professor dropped to his knees and kissed the carved stone, and tears of joy ran down his weathered face. He named the place Port Saknussemm, and he declared in a trembling voice that this was the proof they had waited for, and that they were certainly on the right road. For once, and in spite of all his fears, Axel was obliged to agree with every word that his uncle said.

After a short rest, they went into the tunnel, holding their lamps high so that the light would reach as far as possible. The passage was narrow and its roof was low, but it led steadily downwards, which was precisely what they wanted. Lidenbrock walked ahead with a spring in his step, humming a song from Hamburg.

After a few hundred steps, the lamplight revealed a great heap of fallen rock across the tunnel, as if a giant had emptied a bucket of stones there. It filled the passage from the floor to the roof, and there was no gap through which a mouse could have squeezed. It must have fallen a very long time ago, perhaps during some earthquake that nobody had ever recorded or even known about.

Axel was almost glad, because he thought that this surely was the end of the dangerous adventure, and that they would now have to go home. Lidenbrock, however, refused even to consider turning back, and he stood in front of the rocks with his arms crossed, thinking very hard indeed. A plan, which Axel suspected he would not like at all, was already forming in the Professor's busy and stubborn head.

Lidenbrock drew a small bag from the baggage and opened it to show his nephew the grey powder inside. It was gun-cotton, a violent explosive far stronger than ordinary gunpowder, and the Professor announced calmly that it would blow the fallen rocks to pieces. Axel's face went as white as the cotton itself, and for a moment he could not find any words at all.

Axel protested with all the force that he possessed that the explosion might bring the whole roof of the tunnel down upon their heads. Lidenbrock waved a large hand and replied that a clever man could always use a powerful thing with care and a little courage. He did not seem to hear a single word of the answer, or he chose not to listen to it.

They pushed the gun-cotton into a deep crack between the fallen rocks, and they fixed a long fuse to it with a knot that Hans tied. Hans worked quickly and quietly, with the same steady hands that had built the raft, and he never once glanced at the Professor's face. Axel had the strong feeling, from the hunter's silence, that Hans did not entirely approve of the whole idea.

They unrolled the fuse across the beach until it reached the place where the raft waited at the edge of the water. Lidenbrock explained that it would burn for ten minutes, which would give them time to get away from the blast. Axel asked him how he knew that, and he received in answer a look so withering that he did not ask again.

Somebody had to light the fuse and then run for the raft, and Hans offered to do it, as he offered to do most of the dangerous things on that journey. Lidenbrock agreed at once without a moment's hesitation, and Axel could only hope that the hunter was as fast as he was strong. Axel said a silent prayer for the hunter, and another one, a little longer, for himself and his uncle.

Hans touched a flame to the end of the fuse, and a small bright spark began to creep along the sand towards the rocks. He ran to the raft with long strides, jumped on board, and the three men pushed off together into the dark and silent water. The minutes began to crawl past, one by one, and every one of them seemed to last as long as an hour.

Axel was counting the seconds in his head when the whole cliff seemed to leap into the air with a roar that shook his bones. The explosion was deafening, and a huge flash of light was followed by a hail of stones that fell hissing into the sea around the raft. Then the shock itself came rolling across the cavern, and the whole surface of the sea began to move and to rise.

The explosion had opened a great chasm in the rock, and the sea, which now had no wall to hold it, began to pour into the hole. A mighty wave rose up behind the raft and pushed it towards the edge of the gap as if with a giant hand. Nobody could have stopped it now, however strong or brave or clever, and not even the mighty Hans tried.

The raft was seized by the rushing water, and it spun round and round in a whirlpool that roared like a hundred waterfalls. Then it dropped into the chasm like a leaf into a drain, and the pale light of the cavern vanished above them. Axel felt his stomach rise into his throat as they dropped, and he shut his eyes and held on to the mast with all his might.

For hours the flood carried the raft down a dark tunnel, and the black walls flew past in the lamplight so fast that Axel could not follow them. The air grew steadily hotter with every mile, and he looked at the thermometer with growing fear. The numbers were climbing steadily higher, and none of the three men dared to say aloud what that might mean.

At last the flood began to lose its fury, and the raft came gently to rest in a wide and dark hollow where the water spread out and grew still. For a while the three men lay motionless on the logs, too exhausted to speak, listening to the last of the torrent drain away into the shadows. It was the first real silence that they had known for many hours, and it felt almost as strange as the noise.

Lidenbrock read the thermometer by the light of a lamp, and the number was far higher than any he had written in his notebook before. The heat was so great that the three men could hardly breathe, and sweat ran down their faces and soaked their clothes. Axel remembered his own argument in Hamburg, and a cold, uncomfortable thought struck him.

Then Hans noticed that something was wrong, for the water had stopped falling and was now creeping up the rock wall beside them. He pointed to it without a word, and Axel felt his stomach turn cold as he understood that the flood was no longer taking them down but pushing them up. The Professor frowned deeply and said nothing at all, which was always a sign that he was thinking very hard.

The water lifted the raft higher and higher into a narrow shaft, where the walls seemed to close in around them like the sides of a bottle. Axel realised with a shock that they were no longer travelling downwards at all, but were being carried straight up through the rock by a power that no one could resist. His uncle's face, lit from below by the lamp, was a mask of grim and silent concentration as he watched the walls go by.

The walls were black and scorched, and they were crusted with strange, hard lumps of cooled lava that glittered in the lamplight. Axel stared at them, and slowly, with a dreadful certainty, he understood that they were inside the chimney of a volcano, and that the volcano was awake. He tried to speak and to warn the others, but his mouth was as dry as dust and no sound would come.

A red glow began to shine from far below them, and soon the walls were shaking with a deep and dull roar that Axel could feel in his chest. The water around the raft grew hotter, and a thick, scalding steam rose into the narrow shaft and stung their eyes. Even now, Lidenbrock noted the temperature in his book, with a hand that was as steady as a rock.

The raft shot upwards faster and faster, rocked by the boiling water, and black smoke and flying ash filled the shaft and darkened the lamps. Axel could taste burning in his mouth, and he held on to the mast with both hands so tightly that his fingers lost all feeling. The noise was beyond anything that he had ever heard in his life, and it seemed to fill his whole head.

Axel was quite sure that this was the end, and in his mind he said goodbye to Grauben, to Martha, to Hamburg and to the sun that he would never see again. Lidenbrock took his hand and held it firmly, and Hans simply sat still and waited, as calm as ever. It was a strange comfort to Axel that the other two seemed so calm, and that he did not have to face the end alone.

Then, with a thunderous roar that drowned every other sound, the volcano erupted, and a wall of fire and steam carried the raft upwards like a cork. The three men were thrown high into the air, out of the mouth of the mountain, and for a long moment they seemed to hang there in the light. Then they began to fall together towards the earth and the sunlight, and Axel's last thought was of Grauben.

Axel woke slowly, with a warm sun on his face and soft grass beneath his back, and for a moment he did not know where or even who he was. Hans was sitting beside him, with his usual patient face, and he gave a slow smile when he saw that the young man had at last opened his eyes. It was the sweetest sight in all the world, and Axel felt that he could have wept with gratitude and relief.

The three men were lying on a warm green mountainside, among grapevines, fig trees and wild flowers, under a sky of deep and cloudless blue. The air was soft and sweet and smelt of the sea, and nothing in the landscape resembled Iceland in the slightest. Axel rubbed his eyes again and again, quite certain that he must still be dreaming somewhere in the dark.

They were ravenously hungry, and they ate figs and sweet grapes straight from the branches, scarcely stopping to breathe. Lidenbrock stared around him in bewilderment, his beard stained with juice, and wondered aloud where on Earth they could possibly have arrived. Hans, who seemed to have no such questions at all, simply went on eating figs with a calm and contented face.

Before long some friendly people came down the hillside and offered the strangers bread and wine, laughing at their torn and blackened clothes. Axel understood only a few of their words, but one name was repeated over and over again, and that name was Stromboli. He turned slowly round to look at the smoking peak that stood behind them, and he began to understand.

Stromboli, they discovered, was a volcano on an island off the southern tip of Italy, thousands of kilometres from the cold mountains of Iceland. They sailed across to Messina in Sicily, and from there they made their way home across Europe, by boat and by train. Lidenbrock, who had somehow expected to find the centre of the Earth, spent the whole journey home in silent thought.

When at last they reached Hamburg, Martha opened the door, and she very nearly fainted when she saw who was standing on the step. She had given them up for lost long ago, and she wept and laughed and scolded them all at the same moment. Then, still wiping her eyes on her apron, she hurried away to cook the largest and finest dinner of her whole life.

Grauben ran into the room and straight into Axel's arms, and she told him through her tears that she had waited faithfully for every single day. He held her tightly, with his face in her hair, and he knew that no volcano, sea or professor in the world would ever make him leave her again. For a long while they laughed and cried together in the sunny room, and neither of them said anything sensible at all.

News of the journey spread rapidly, and Lidenbrock became one of the most celebrated scientists in all of Germany, invited to lecture in every great hall. Axel's account of their adventures was read by thousands of people who could hardly believe a word of it, and he found himself quite famous too. Soon afterwards he married Grauben in a joyful wedding, to the delight of the whole family and of Martha in particular.

Later, Axel explained to his uncle that the lightning had turned the needle of the compass right round, so that for many days they had been steering in the wrong direction. That was why they had never reached the true centre of the Earth, and Lidenbrock accepted the explanation with a long sigh. He admitted, a little sadly, that science sometimes had surprises even for the men who loved it most and served it best.

Hans took his pay, thanked the Professor in his quiet way, and went home to Iceland, as unhurried and calm as on the day that he had first arrived. The others never forgot the silent hunter who had carried them through so much danger, and Axel thought of him whenever anyone spoke the word brave. He never learned what Hans had really thought of the two noisy foreigners and their wonderful, foolish journey underground.

Of course, no one could really make this journey, for the Earth grows steadily hotter beneath our feet, and its centre is a place of enormous heat and pressure. The deepest hole that people have ever drilled reaches only about twelve kilometres, while the centre lies roughly 6,400 kilometres down. Yet this tale of daring and wonder has carried readers into the dark for generations, and it still invites them to ask what lies below.
